I'd say most of this depends on your climate, and your land availability.. What sort of success rate do trees and bees have when starting out in your area? Sounds like you're in a rural area, so consider asking neighbors for advice.

Greenhouse: Depends on your growing season. If you already grow cash crops that are only one zone out of their ideal zone, a frugally constructed greenhouse could pay itself off quickly. Some transplant-able crops may also become economical with an indoor start in the fall.

Bees: Check locally. They take a lot of time/effort, making them a poor money-making choice at a small scale. If you live across from a mega-farm, bees might fail. Some pesticides are bad for them. Plant the right flowers in the general area and you'll support more bees. That's about all I know.

Chickens: More cost effective when you have some space to keep roosters separate so you can breed them and raise chicks. Young hens themselves might be sold, depending on local laws. Some cover crops can be tossed about at random to grow supplemental feed. Manure has obvious benefits. Just make sure you can justify the savings on eggs/poultry against the cost of feeding the birds.

Also, you might be able to build a culvert to irrigate a pipe under a potential greenhouse, but that depends on the topography, and your budget.

Bees and stone fruits do well here. Apples do extremely well, but there are so many orchards that there is no profit. The whole area was originally planned out as a bread basket to supply miners, with the original name being Fruitland.

The greenhouse is mostly meant to store planted crops like strawberries. I can produce about 1k potted strawberries for wholesale to local nurseries, but don't have space to keep the pots warm. The irrigation would be drip irrigation.

Bees do fine here, and there are no large farms around. I probably won't go the bee route though, as even in the middle of winter I've got bees swarming around the early flowers. I dont think it will actually have a huge impact on production.

Chickens do seem to be the best bet. The amount of compost I produce, along with cover crops, should keep them well fed. In addition, having them roam the yard to eat the inevitable grasshoppers and catapillars would cut down on plant damage.

Based on all that, it sounds like fruit trees might be a good second or third round investment if they aren't very marketable in your area. They'll still eventually save you money on food, but wont net you any real immediate income that could help with further developing your land.

The greenhouse could pay itself off in a growing season if it enabled you to sell more plants. It depends on factors like greenhouse cost, greenhouse capacity, and how many potted plants you can sell. Is there a significant reason you can't do drip irrigation in the greenhouse? There are lots of inventive DIY systems for nearly every situation. I'm not sure what a potted strawberry plant sells for to a nursery, but I could imagine the cost of an irrigation system being recouped pretty quickly. This all obviously depends on the cost of those licenses and inspections you mentioned

Since selling bulk plants isn't in your budget this season, I agree that chickens seem to be your safest, best bet. They provide more immediate benefits. Just do your homework and chickens should be easy. Just be sure to protect them from any predators.

Best of luck on your property! I'm sure we'd all love to hear back from you as your homestead grows.

This was the last song Croce played before his death. He performed it as an encore at show in Natchitoches, Louisiana at Northwestern College. The crowd was small, as many folks stayed home to watch the Billie Jean King vs. Bobby Riggs "Battle of the Sexes" tennis match that night. Croce's plane, taking off in the dark after the concert, clipped a tree and crashed, killing all six people on board.

This is a rare song that Croce recorded but did not write. Ingrid Croce, who was married to Jim from 1966 until his death in 1973, told us: "It was written by Norman Gimbel and Charles Fox. And they were wonderful guys, really nice people. Jim had been selected to sing this song for this particular movie. He really enjoyed this opportunity, because he went into the recording studio and it was a little awkward for him not to hold his guitar - his guitar is kind of like a bar for the bartender, having that prop between him and the audience was just a real security, it made him feel very comfortable. So putting down the guitar to sing, just to sing the song in the studio, was a very unusual thing for Jim, and he thoroughly enjoyed it. It was a brand new start for him in some ways, to use his vocals in a different way. I think it's one of the most powerful songs he does on that album for sure. I loved it." Explaining how this song was a good fit for her husband, Ingrid says: "More people think he wrote that song. His voice was so unique... the timbre in his tone and his warmth and his generosity, everything came through that voice. So when he took a song, he'd make it his own, and I think he did a great job with 'I've Got A Name.' So many people like to think of Jim with that song that I hate to tell them it isn't his."

According to Rick Derringer, the original version of Sloopy was written by a "high school kid in St. Louis" and sold to Bert Russell, a.k.a. Bert Berns. If true, the answer to the age old question "Just who is Sloopy?" lies with him. Dorothy Sloop, a jazz singer from Steubenville and a student at Ohio University, is said to be the inspiration for the song.

In early 1965, The Strangeloves, a New York City rock band, wanted to make the song the follow-up to their hit single "I Want Candy" and began performing the song in concert. However, the Dave Clark Five, with whom they were touring, told the Strangeloves that they were going to record their own version of the song when they returned to England, copying the Strangeloves' crowd-pleasing arrangement. The Strangeloves realized that the Dave Clark Five's version would probably outsell their own, but they weren't ready to release a new single yet because they were still enjoying the success of "I Want Candy" from a few months earlier. The answer presented itself when a young rock group named Rick and the Raiders opened for (and provided backing for) The Strangeloves in July in Dayton, Ohio. The Strangeloves — who were, in reality, three successful writer/producers from Brooklyn, New York — recruited Rick and The Raiders to release the song under their name. Their 16-year-old leader, Rick Zehringer, was flown to New York to record his lead vocal over The Strangeloves' already-recorded backing tracks. It was decided to change the name of Rick's group to The McCoys to avoid confusion with another popular band of the era, Paul Revere & the Raiders, and Rick himself began using the stage name Rick Derringer.

Originally written and recorded with three verses, the newly retitled "Hang On Sloopy" was edited down to two verses for the single and resulting Hang On Sloopy album.
